title: How Many Is Enough
subtitle: A child with repeated sore throats, from the referral letter to the follow-up visit
description: Counting episodes against the documentation criteria, deciding whether to offer surgery, same-day discharge versus overnight monitoring, what goes in at induction, discharge analgesia, and what to tell the family afterward.

steps.title: Step 1/6: Counting Episodes
steps.scenario:
An 8-year-old girl is referred for recurrent sore throat. Her mother says she has had more than ten this year and has been on antibiotics repeatedly.

You pull the records. There are nine clinic visits for sore throat in the past 12 months:

    4 visits    sore throat, temperature 38.6 to 39.2 C documented
    2 visits    sore throat, tonsillar exudate described
    1 visit     sore throat, rapid group A strep test positive
    2 visits    "sore throat, antibiotic prescribed" and nothing else recorded
steps.media: Load image: Oropharyngeal photograph showing enlarged tonsils with exudate. Caption: 'Oropharynx.'
steps.question: How many of these episodes count toward the criteria for tonsillectomy?

options.text: (A) Nine, because every clinic visit for sore throat in the past year counts
(B) More than ten, because the mother's account also covers episodes managed at home
(C) Seven
(D) One, because only a positive group A strep test confirms an episode

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

An episode counts only when the record for that visit documents a sore throat plus at least one of the following: temperature above 38.3 C (101 F), cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or a positive test for group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. Four visits qualify on temperature, two on exudate, and one on the strep test. The remaining two record a sore throat and a prescription and nothing else.

Why the others fail:
(A) A visit for sore throat is not the same as a qualifying episode. Most sore throats at this age are viral, and the four listed features are what separate the episodes the trials counted from the rest.
(B) The requirement is not there to doubt the mother. It is there because the trials that showed benefit enrolled children whose episodes had these documented features. Counting episodes that were never characterized brings in children who were not represented in those trials, and the expected benefit does not transfer.
(D) A positive strep test is one of four acceptable features, not the only one. Fever, adenopathy and exudate each qualify on their own, and in practice most documented episodes qualify on fever or exudate rather than on a swab.

Keypoint: an episode counts when the chart records a sore throat plus one of four specific findings, not when the family remembers it.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Tonsillectomy in Children (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42. doi:10.1177/0194599818801757, Key Action Statement 2.

steps.title: Step 2/6: What You Recommend
steps.scenario:
Seven documented qualifying episodes in the past 12 months.

She is otherwise well and growing normally. She does not snore and there is no witnessed apnea. She has no drug allergies and no bleeding history.
steps.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Offer tonsillectomy, and decide with the family
(B) Watchful waiting, since the criterion requires seven episodes across two years rather than in one
(C) Watchful waiting, since she has had no complications from any of the episodes
(D) Six months of prophylactic antibiotics, then reconsider surgery

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Seven documented episodes in the past year meets the frequency criterion, and tonsillectomy becomes a reasonable option. Note the strength of the statement: this is an option, not a strong recommendation. Meeting the criterion makes surgery defensible, not obligatory, and the decision is made with the family after discussing the expected benefit and the risks.

Why the others fail:
(B) Misreads the three thresholds. They are seven episodes in the past year, or five per year for two years, or three per year for three years. Any one of the three is sufficient, and she meets the first.
(C) Complications are not part of the frequency criterion. A history of more than one peritonsillar abscess is one of the factors that can justify surgery in a child who falls below the thresholds, but their absence does not disqualify a child who meets them.
(D) Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis is not part of this guideline. It exposes her to adverse effects and resistance, and it does not change the fact that she already meets the criterion.

Keypoint: meeting the criterion opens the conversation about surgery rather than settling it.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42, Key Action Statements 2 and 3.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Home the Same Day
steps.scenario:
The family agrees to surgery. She is 8 years old, has no obstructive symptoms and no comorbid conditions, and lives 40 minutes from the hospital.

The list is a day surgery list.
steps.question: Does she need overnight inpatient monitoring?

options.text: (A) Yes, because the first 24 hours carry the risk of primary bleeding
(B) Yes, because all children under 12 are observed overnight after tonsillectomy
(C) Yes, because of the number of throat infections she has had
(D) No, overnight monitoring is for children under 3 years or with severe obstructive sleep apnea

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Overnight inpatient monitoring is recommended for children younger than 3 years, and for children with severe obstructive sleep apnea, defined as an apnea-hypopnea index of 10 or more obstructive events per hour, an oxygen saturation nadir below 80 percent, or both. She is 8, has no obstructive symptoms, and meets neither. Same-day discharge is appropriate.

Why the others fail:
(A) The reasoning sounds protective and does not hold. Primary bleeding is uncommon, and an overnight stay does not prevent it; it only changes where the child is if it happens. The criteria are built around airway risk after surgery, not around bleeding surveillance.
(B) There is no age cutoff of 12. The stated age criterion is under 3 years.
(C) The number of preoperative infections says nothing about the risk of the postoperative night. It was the reason for the operation, not a reason to admit.

Keypoint: the overnight criteria are about airway risk, and they are age under 3 or severe sleep apnea.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42, Key Action Statement 12.

steps.title: Step 4/6: At Induction
steps.scenario: She is on the table. Anesthesia asks what you want given.
steps.question: What do you give intraoperatively?

options.text: (A) A single dose of intravenous antibiotic, and no steroid
(B) A single dose of intravenous dexamethasone, and no antibiotic
(C) Both a single dose of dexamethasone and a single dose of intravenous antibiotic
(D) Neither, since both have been linked to increased postoperative bleeding

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Two separate strong recommendations point in opposite directions. A single intraoperative dose of intravenous dexamethasone should be given: it reduces postoperative nausea and vomiting and improves early oral intake. Perioperative antibiotics should not be given or prescribed: they do not reduce pain, bleeding, or return visits, and they carry the usual costs of resistance and adverse effects.

Why the others fail:
(A) Reverses both recommendations at once.
(C) The steroid half is correct. The antibiotic half is the part practice has moved away from, and it was one of the statements revised in 2019 because routine use had persisted without benefit.
(D) The concern about steroids and bleeding is the reason this was studied in the first place. A single intraoperative dose has not been shown to increase bleeding that requires intervention, and withholding it gives up a benefit that is well established.

Keypoint: give the steroid, withhold the antibiotic, and note that both are strong recommendations rather than preferences.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42, Key Action Statements 10 and 11.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Going Home
steps.scenario:
The operation is uncomplicated. She wakes well, drinks, and is ready for discharge the same afternoon.

Her mother asks what to give her for the pain.
steps.question: What do you prescribe?

options.text: (A) Ibuprofen, acetaminophen, or both
(B) Acetaminophen with codeine at weight-based dosing
(C) Acetaminophen alone, since ibuprofen increases the risk of post-tonsillectomy bleeding
(D) Acetaminophen with tramadol, which avoids the known problem with codeine

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Ibuprofen, acetaminophen, or both is a strong recommendation. Used together they control pain well enough that most children do not need an opioid at all, which is the point.

Why the others fail:
(B) Codeine must not be given to any child under 12 after tonsillectomy. Codeine is converted to morphine by CYP2D6, some children are ultra-rapid metabolizers, and deaths from respiratory depression have been reported in exactly this setting. This is one of only two prohibitions in the guideline.
(C) A widely held belief that the evidence does not support. Ibuprofen has not been shown to increase post-tonsillectomy bleeding that requires intervention. Withholding it gives weaker analgesia and pushes families toward opioids, which is the greater risk.
(D) Tramadol is also metabolized by CYP2D6 and carries the same ultra-rapid metabolizer problem as codeine. It is not the safe substitute it is often assumed to be, and it is restricted in children after tonsillectomy for the same reason.

Keypoint: the two non-opioids are the first-line prescription, and codeine and tramadol share the same metabolic reason for being avoided.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42, Key Action Statements 13 and 14.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Six Weeks Later
steps.scenario:
She had a sore throat for about ten days and then settled. There was no bleeding.

At her six-week visit the fossae are healed. Her mother asks whether this means the sore throats are over.
steps.media: Load image: Oropharyngeal photograph showing healed tonsillar fossae. Caption: 'Six weeks.'
steps.question: What do you tell her?

options.text: (A) She should not get throat infections again, since the tonsils have been removed
(B) Her immune defenses will now be weaker, so she should expect more infections of other kinds
(C) The reduction is real but modest and is concentrated in the first year or two, and recurrent throat infection tends to become less frequent over time even without surgery
(D) Tonsillectomy has not been shown to reduce throat infections, and it was done mainly to shorten each episode

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Both halves of this matter. Tonsillectomy does reduce the frequency of throat infection in severely affected children, but the size of the effect is modest and largest in the first year or two. At the same time, recurrent throat infection improves on its own with age, which is the reason the thresholds for operating are set as high as they are.

Why the others fail:
(A) Removing the tonsils does not remove the pharynx. She can still get pharyngitis, including streptococcal pharyngitis, and promising otherwise sets up a conversation you will have to take back.
(B) A common family worry and worth answering directly. No study has demonstrated a clinically significant effect of tonsillectomy on immune function.
(D) Understates a real effect. The benefit in frequency exists in children who meet the criteria; it is the size of it, not its existence, that gets overstated.

Keypoint: promise a smaller number of sore throats, not the end of them, and say that some of the improvement would have come anyway.

Reference: Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42. Paradise JL, Bluestone CD, Bachman RZ, et al. Efficacy of tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in severely affected children. N Engl J Med. 1984;310(11):674-683.
